titlePl: Matura PR: Miejsce zamieszkania — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Home — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Miejsce zamieszkania na maturę rozszerzoną: mieszkalnictwo, urbanizacja, sąsiedztwo i problemy mieszkaniowe. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended Matura Home module: housing, urban life, neighbourhoods and housing problems. ENG–PL flashcards.

items.definitionEn: an old multi-storey building divided into rented flats, often in a city centre
items.example: Many students rent rooms in a pre-war tenement near the university.

items.definitionEn: a high-status flat on the top floor of a building, usually with a terrace
items.example: A penthouse with a skyline view is far beyond a first-time buyer's budget.

items.definitionEn: homes provided by the local authority at lower rent for people on low incomes
items.example: Waiting lists for council housing can stretch for years in large cities.

items.definitionEn: a small flat in which the living room and bedroom share one space
items.example: A studio flat is cheaper, but the lack of privacy becomes exhausting.

items.definitionEn: a single rented room used for both living and sleeping, with basic cooking facilities
items.example: He spent his first year in a damp bedsit above a noisy shop.

items.definitionEn: a tall residential building with many floors of flats
items.example: Children in a high-rise block may have no safe place to play downstairs.

items.definitionEn: a very tall block of flats, often associated with post-war housing estates
items.example: A neglected tower block can become a symbol of urban decay.

items.definitionEn: a flat on two floors with its own internal stairs, usually in a larger building
items.example: The maisonette has a small garden that a mid-floor flat would lack.

items.definitionEn: an attic turned into extra living space
items.example: A loft conversion added a study without the cost of moving house.

items.definitionEn: a former industrial building turned into flats
items.example: Artists moved into a converted warehouse long before the cafés arrived.

items.definitionEn: an older house with historic architectural features
items.example: They restored a period property with original wooden floors.

items.definitionEn: a small country house with a roof made of straw or reeds
items.example: A thatched cottage looks charming, but insurance and upkeep are expensive.

items.definitionEn: the main house on a farm
items.example: They restored a farmhouse and now commute to the city twice a week.

items.definitionEn: a building of rooms for students, usually run by a university
items.example: Life in a hall of residence teaches you more about compromise than any textbook.

items.definitionEn: a flat or house in which unrelated people rent rooms together
items.example: Bills in shared accommodation should be written into the tenancy agreement.

items.definitionEn: flats for elderly or vulnerable people with some on-site support
items.example: Sheltered housing allowed her grandmother to stay independent without isolation.

items.definitionEn: a prefabricated dwelling that can be moved, often on a permanent site
items.example: A mobile home on the edge of town was the only option they could afford.

items.definitionEn: a house built from factory-made sections assembled on site
items.example: A prefabricated house can be weatherproof in weeks rather than months.

items.definitionEn: a home that has just been constructed and not lived in before
items.example: A newly built property may still have snagging problems in the first year.

items.definitionEn: an additional property used for holidays or investment, not as a main residence
items.example: Villagers complain that a second home sits empty for ten months a year.

items.definitionEn: a home bought in order to rent it out rather than live in it
items.example: Investors chasing a buy-to-let property push prices beyond local wages.

items.definitionEn: a residential area with controlled entrances and private security
items.example: A gated community can feel safe, yet it weakens everyday contact with the town.

items.definitionEn: a planned area of houses or blocks built as a single development
items.example: The housing estate has a playground but no shop within walking distance.

items.definitionEn: previously developed land, often industrial, reused for new housing
items.example: Building on a brownfield site spares countryside but may require decontamination.

items.definitionEn: land that has not been built on before, usually countryside or fields
items.example: Opponents say a greenfield site should not be sacrificed to urban sprawl.

items.definitionEn: a row of houses that share side walls with their neighbours
items.example: Terraced housing is dense, which can mean both community and thin walls.

items.definitionEn: a house that stands alone and does not share walls with another dwelling
items.example: A detached property on the outskirts often means a long commute.

items.definitionPl: mieszkanie w budynku zaprojektowanym jako blok
items.definitionEn: an apartment constructed as a flat from the start, not converted from a house
items.example: A purpose-built flat usually has better soundproofing than a converted tenement.

items.definitionEn: a project combining housing with shops, offices or public services
items.example: A mixed-use development can reduce commuting if the jobs are genuine.

items.definitionEn: a new group of houses or flats built by a developer
items.example: The residential development promised amenities that still have not opened.

items.definitionEn: a community of private homes with shared facilities and joint decisions
items.example: A co-housing scheme can ease loneliness among both students and pensioners.

items.definitionPl: mieszkanie dla seniora przy domu rodziny
items.definitionEn: a small self-contained dwelling attached to or in the garden of a family house
items.example: A granny flat let her father stay close without sacrificing everyone's privacy.

items.definitionEn: a flat partly or wholly below street level
items.example: A basement flat can be dark and prone to rising damp.

items.definitionEn: a flat on the top floor, often with sloping ceilings
items.example: An attic flat is cheaper, but there is no lift and the rooms overheat in summer.

items.definitionEn: a ground-floor apartment with access to a garden
items.example: A garden flat is ideal with a dog, provided the fence is solid.

items.definitionEn: an organisation whose members jointly own and manage their housing
items.example: A housing cooperative can keep rents lower than a private landlord would.

items.definitionEn: designed as one large space rather than separate rooms
items.example: An open-plan kitchen is sociable, but cooking smells reach the sofa.

items.definitionEn: a system that warms a room through pipes or cables beneath the floor
items.example: Underfloor heating is pleasant, yet it is slow to adjust on a sudden cold night.

items.definitionEn: a kitchen with cupboards and appliances built to fill the space
items.example: The landlord advertised a fitted kitchen that turned out to be fifteen years old.

items.definitionEn: a wardrobe constructed as part of the wall, not a free-standing piece
items.example: A built-in wardrobe saves floor space in a studio flat.

items.definitionEn: a private bathroom attached to a bedroom
items.example: An ensuite bathroom makes shared accommodation far easier to live with.

items.definitionEn: a small room used only for storing and organising clothes
items.example: A walk-in wardrobe is a luxury that most city rents will not stretch to.

items.definitionEn: a glass room attached to a house, used for sitting and plants
items.example: The conservatory is unusable in August without blinds.

items.definitionEn: an underground room used for storage, often cooler than the house
items.example: Bicycles and winter coats live in the cellar because the flat has no storage space.

items.definitionEn: a small room or cupboard for storing food
items.example: A pantry next to the kitchen beats cramming packets into a single cupboard.

items.definitionEn: an extra partial floor between two main storeys
items.example: A mezzanine sleeping area works in a loft but can feel exposed to guests.

items.definitionEn: a window set into the roof
items.example: A skylight brightens an attic flat, yet it can leak after heavy snow.

items.definitionEn: a window that sticks out from the wall, creating an alcove inside
items.example: A bay window with a window seat became the only quiet corner to revise.

items.definitionEn: windows with two layers of glass to reduce heat loss and noise
items.example: Double glazing finally made homework possible next to the ring road.

items.definitionEn: material that stops heat escaping from a building
items.example: Poor insulation is a major cause of fuel poverty in older tenements.

items.definitionEn: the device that heats water for radiators and taps
items.example: When the boiler broke in January, the landlord took a week to send a plumber.

items.definitionEn: the panel that controls and protects a building's electrical circuits
items.example: The fuse box is in the hall, so a power cut means groping for a torch.

items.definitionEn: a device that removes steam and cooking smells from a room
items.example: Without an extractor fan, mould spread across the bathroom ceiling.

items.definitionEn: a device that sounds an alarm when it senses smoke
items.example: Every rented property should have a working smoke detector on each floor.

items.definitionEn: a security system that sounds if someone breaks in
items.example: A burglar alarm is little use if the tenants forget to set it.

items.definitionEn: a speaker system used to let visitors into a building
items.example: The intercom has been broken for months, so couriers ring random flats.

items.definitionEn: a floor made of small wooden blocks arranged in a pattern
items.example: Original parquet flooring was one reason they chose the pre-war tenement.

items.definitionEn: a factory-made floor covering that imitates wood
items.example: Laminate flooring is cheap, but downstairs neighbours hear every footstep.

items.definitionEn: original decorative details from the time a building was constructed
items.example: Buyers pay extra for period features such as ceiling roses and panelled doors.

items.definitionEn: interior walls left as bare brick for a decorative industrial look
items.example: Exposed brickwork looks stylish until you try to hang a bookshelf.

items.definitionEn: a shower with a pump that produces a strong flow of water
items.example: A power shower is advertised as a luxury and then restricted by weak water pressure.

items.definitionEn: room in a home for keeping belongings
items.example: The biggest complaint about studio flats is the lack of storage space.

items.definitionEn: stairs shared by several flats in a building
items.example: Nobody wants to be the one who cleans the communal staircase.

items.definitionEn: an external staircase or route for leaving a building during a fire
items.example: The landlord had blocked the fire escape with bicycles.

items.definitionEn: outdoor space shared by residents of a block or estate
items.example: A communal garden can create a sense of community if people actually use it.

items.definitionEn: a device that records energy use in real time and sends readings automatically
items.example: A smart meter made the tenants realise how much heating they were wasting.

items.definitionEn: a system that extracts heat from air or ground to warm a building
items.example: A heat pump is efficient in a well-insulated house and disappointing in a draughty one.

items.definitionEn: a fast internet service supplied to a home
items.example: Without a stable broadband connection, remote learning from a village is a lottery.

items.definitionEn: a barrier in a wall that stops moisture rising from the ground
items.example: The surveyor noted that the damp-proof course had failed in two rooms.

items.definitionEn: material pumped into the gap between two layers of an outside wall to keep heat in
items.example: Cavity wall insulation cut their heating bills by almost a third.

items.definitionPl: szafa na pościel przy piecu / suszarnia
items.definitionEn: a warm cupboard, often around the hot-water tank, used to dry linen
items.example: Towels dry overnight in the airing cupboard next to the boiler.

items.definitionEn: a high counter where people can sit and eat in the kitchen
items.example: An open-plan breakfast bar replaced the separate dining room.

items.definitionEn: a free-standing worktop in the middle of a kitchen
items.example: A kitchen island looks impressive and then blocks every useful walking route.

items.definitionEn: fridges, ovens and similar machines built into kitchen units
items.example: The rent is higher because the flat comes with fitted appliances.

items.definitionEn: a shower area you enter without stepping over a high tray
items.example: A walk-in shower is easier for a frail resident than a high bath.

items.definitionEn: a fully waterproofed bathroom in which the shower has no separate tray
items.example: A wet room is practical, but a single blocked drain floods the whole floor.

items.definitionEn: useful facilities such as shops, parks, schools and clinics near a home
items.example: The brochure promised amenities that turned out to be a single corner shop.

items.definitionEn: everyday services available in the immediate neighbourhood
items.example: Young families look first at local amenities, not at the kitchen island.

items.definitionEn: close enough to reach on foot in a reasonable time
items.example: If the station is not within walking distance, the cheap rent is a false economy.

items.definitionEn: having convenient transport links to other places
items.example: A well-connected suburb can be more practical than a fashionable but isolated loft.

items.definitionEn: having few or unreliable buses and trains
items.example: Villages poorly served by public transport force teenagers to depend on parents.

items.definitionEn: parks, squares and other vegetated public areas in a town
items.example: Access to green space is uneven between inner-city wards.

items.definitionEn: the main shopping street of a town
items.example: When the high street loses its last bank, older residents are stranded.

items.definitionEn: a street closed at one end, with no through traffic
items.example: Parents like a cul-de-sac because children can play with less traffic.

items.definitionEn: too many vehicles on the roads, causing slow movement
items.example: Traffic congestion in the commuter belt starts before seven in the morning.

items.definitionEn: a marked part of the road reserved for bicycles
items.example: A painted cycle lane that cars ignore is a political gesture, not infrastructure.

items.definitionEn: a street or area where cars are not allowed
items.example: A pedestrianised zone revived cafés but complicated deliveries to residents.

items.definitionEn: the regular service that takes household rubbish away
items.example: Irregular refuse collection turned the courtyard into an unofficial dump.

items.definitionEn: towns and suburbs from which people travel daily to work in a city
items.example: House prices in the commuter belt rose as soon as the fast train opened.

items.definitionEn: a town whose residents mostly work elsewhere and return only to sleep
items.example: A dormitory town can feel empty on weekdays and overcrowded at weekends.

items.definitionEn: the central area of a city, often denser and sometimes poorer than the suburbs
items.example: Inner city schools face overcrowding that suburban campuses rarely see.

items.definitionEn: a quiet residential area outside the centre, with trees and gardens
items.example: A leafy suburb offers space, at the cost of commuting from the suburbs.

items.definitionEn: a neighbourhood in poor physical and social condition
items.example: Artists often arrive in a rundown area just before gentrification begins.

items.definitionEn: a neighbourhood that is becoming more fashionable and expensive
items.example: Rents in an up-and-coming area can double within a few years.

items.definitionEn: an idealised picture of peaceful country life
items.example: The rural idyll collapses when the last bus is cancelled in October.

items.definitionEn: the way of living associated with cities: density, services, noise and choice
items.example: An urban lifestyle suits students until they want a garden and silence.

items.definitionEn: how fast or slow everyday living feels in a place
items.example: The pace of life in a market town can feel either calming or claustrophobic.

items.definitionEn: the feeling that neighbours know and support one another
items.example: A sense of community is harder to build in a block where people never meet.

items.definitionEn: a local scheme in which residents look out for crime and report it
items.example: The neighbourhood watch group also organised a street clean-up.

items.definitionPl: sąsiad zza ściany / z domu obok
items.definitionEn: the person living in the adjoining house or flat
items.example: A considerate next-door neighbour is worth more than a designer kitchen.

items.definitionPl: żyć na swoim, nie wdawać się w życie sąsiadów
items.definitionEn: to avoid social contact with neighbours and live privately
items.example: In a big city it is easy to keep yourself to yourself and never learn names.

items.definitionEn: bus, rail and road connections from a place to other areas
items.example: Poor transport links can isolate a new housing estate from jobs and schools.

items.definitionEn: the zone around a school or hospital that determines who may use it
items.example: Families move house simply to enter a better school's catchment area.

items.definitionEn: a pedestrian area or small centre with a group of shops
items.example: The shopping precinct is convenient, yet it killed the independent high street.

items.definitionEn: public lamps that make roads and pavements visible at night
items.example: Residents demanded better street lighting after a series of thefts.

items.definitionEn: a very small rural settlement far from towns and services
items.example: An isolated hamlet may have beauty and no doctor within twenty kilometres.

items.definitionEn: a public field used for sport and play
items.example: The recreation ground is the only free meeting place for teenagers on the estate.

items.definitionEn: a car park on the edge of a town from which buses take people into the centre
items.example: A park-and-ride scheme reduced traffic congestion in the old town.

items.definitionEn: a main road that goes around a town rather than through its centre
items.example: The ring road moved lorries out of the high street but split a housing estate in two.

items.definitionEn: an area where people are friendly and often spend time together
items.example: A convivial neighbourhood can compensate for a cramped flat.

items.definitionEn: places such as theatres, libraries and galleries in an area
items.example: Without cultural facilities, a dormitory town offers little except sleep.

items.definitionEn: clinics, hospitals and other medical services available locally
items.example: New estates often appear before healthcare facilities have been funded.

items.definitionEn: too many people living in a space that is too small
items.example: Overcrowding in student flats is treated as a joke until exam season arrives.

items.definitionEn: the process by which wealthier people move in and prices push original residents out
items.example: Gentrification replaced the bakery with a café that locals cannot afford.

items.definitionEn: the condition of having no secure place to live
items.example: Homelessness is not only sleeping rough; it includes unstable temporary rooms.

items.definitionEn: the unplanned spread of a city into surrounding countryside
items.example: Urban sprawl destroys farmland and makes car travel almost compulsory.

items.definitionEn: travelling daily from an outer residential area into the city for work or school
items.example: Commuting from the suburbs costs her three hours a day and a season ticket.

items.definitionEn: a lack of enough homes for the people who need them
items.example: A housing shortage lets landlords raise rents with little fear of empty flats.

items.definitionEn: house and flat prices that are rising rapidly
items.example: Soaring property prices have locked a generation out of ownership.

items.definitionEn: homes that cost more than local people can reasonably pay
items.example: Unaffordable housing forces graduates to stay in their childhood bedrooms.

items.definitionEn: homes that are unsafe, unhealthy or below legal quality standards
items.example: Charities document substandard housing with mould, faulty wiring and no heating.

items.definitionEn: moisture that travels up walls from the ground, causing stains and decay
items.example: Rising damp ruined the downstairs plaster within a single winter.

items.definitionEn: a fungus that grows in damp rooms and can damage health
items.example: Mould behind the wardrobe is a health issue, not a cosmetic one.

items.definitionEn: a large number of insects or vermin living in a building
items.example: An infestation of mice is grounds for demanding repairs from the landlord.

items.definitionEn: harmful or annoying levels of sound in the environment
items.example: Noise pollution from the ring road made the cheap rent far less attractive.

items.definitionEn: a shared place in a block where residents leave rubbish
items.example: Please take cardboard to the communal bin store, not the hallway.

items.definitionEn: deliberate damage to property
items.example: Vandalism in the communal staircase made residents feel unsafe at night.

items.definitionEn: conduct that causes alarm, distress or nuisance to other people
items.example: Persistent antisocial behaviour can justify eviction, but the process is slow.

items.definitionEn: an empty structure in a very bad state of repair
items.example: A derelict building on the high street dragged the whole street's reputation down.

items.definitionEn: a house or flat that is empty and not being lived in
items.example: Taxing vacant property is one proposed answer to the housing shortage.

items.definitionEn: the legal process of forcing a tenant to leave a property
items.example: An eviction for rent arrears can push a family into homelessness.

items.definitionEn: a period when property prices rise far above real value and then risk collapsing
items.example: Economists warn that a housing bubble leaves young buyers with negative equity.

items.definitionPl: ujemny kapitał (kredyt wyższy niż wartość mieszkania)
items.definitionEn: the situation in which a mortgage is larger than the home's market value
items.example: Negative equity trapped them in a flat they could neither sell nor remortgage.

items.definitionEn: being unable to afford adequate heating without cutting other essentials
items.example: Fuel poverty is common in poorly insulated tenements with expensive electric heating.

items.definitionPl: spać na ulicy / bez dachu nad głową
items.definitionEn: spending the night outdoors because you have no home
items.example: Charities count people sleeping rough, but many more are hidden in unstable rooms.

items.definitionEn: staying temporarily on friends' sofas because you have no home of your own
items.example: Sofa-surfing is a form of hidden homelessness among young people.

items.definitionEn: an official queue for social or council housing
items.example: Families can spend a decade on a housing waiting list in the capital.

items.definitionPl: dzielnica o wysokim ubóstwie / deficycie usług
items.definitionEn: a neighbourhood with high poverty and poor services
items.example: A deprived area may be a bus ride from wealth and still lack a GP surgery.

items.definitionEn: a housing estate with severe social problems and a poor reputation
items.example: Calling a place a sink estate can stigmatise residents who have no other choice.

items.definitionEn: the process by which buildings and public spaces in a city fall into neglect
items.example: Urban decay and empty shops feed each other once the last bank closes.

items.definitionEn: planned investment to improve a declining urban area
items.example: Regeneration that ignores existing tenants is just another name for gentrification.

items.definitionEn: the inability to be unseen or uninterrupted in your own home
items.example: A lack of privacy is the hidden cost of shared accommodation.

items.definitionEn: poorly insulated walls that let sound pass between homes
items.example: Thin walls mean you learn your next-door neighbour's timetable by accident.

items.definitionEn: people living nearby who disturb others with loud sound
items.example: Mediation failed, so the tenants reported the noisy neighbours to the council.

items.definitionEn: official approval required before constructing or significantly altering a building
items.example: They could not add a conservatory without planning permission.

items.definitionEn: opposition to new housing or infrastructure near one's own home, while accepting it elsewhere
items.example: Nimbyism can block the very homes that would ease a local housing shortage.

items.definitionEn: a legal disagreement about where one property ends and another begins
items.example: A boundary dispute over a fence lasted longer than the friendship next door.

items.definitionPl: lokal zamieszkany przez kilka niezwiązanych gospodarstw (HMO)
items.definitionEn: a property rented room by room to three or more unrelated people sharing facilities
items.example: A house in multiple occupation needs extra fire safety checks.

items.definitionEn: a long-term bank loan used to buy a home, secured on the property
items.example: Without a stable income it is almost impossible to obtain a mortgage.

items.definitionEn: a sum paid to a landlord as security, usually returned if the property is left in good condition
items.example: The landlord kept part of the deposit because the walls were damaged.

items.definitionEn: the person or company that owns a property and rents it to others
items.example: A responsible landlord replies to repair requests within days, not months.

items.definitionEn: a person who pays rent to live in a property owned by someone else
items.example: A tenant has a right to a safe home, even in the cheapest studio flat.

items.definitionEn: a woman who owns a property and rents it to tenants
items.example: Their landlady lived upstairs and complained about every late-night guest.

items.definitionEn: a company that finds tenants and manages rented property for the owner
items.example: The letting agency charged both sides and still lost the keys twice.

items.definitionEn: a professional who markets homes for sale or rent and shows them to clients
items.example: An estate agent described the noisy road as 'well-connected'.

items.definitionEn: the legal contract between landlord and tenant setting out the terms of the let
items.example: Read the tenancy agreement before you pay a deposit you may never see again.

items.definitionEn: a formal warning that a tenancy will end
items.example: The landlord sent a notice to quit after unpaid rent.

items.definitionEn: a tenant already living in a property, often with strong legal protection
items.example: A sitting tenant can make a house harder to sell and sometimes safer to occupy.

items.definitionEn: unpaid rent that a tenant owes
items.example: Rent arrears of two months triggered a warning letter from the letting agency.

items.definitionEn: an arrangement in which utilities are covered by the rent rather than paid separately
items.example: A room with bills included is easier to budget for, even if the rent looks higher.

items.definitionEn: a local tax on residential property that funds council services
items.example: Students in a hall of residence are usually exempt from council tax.

items.definitionEn: a tax paid when buying a property above a certain price
items.example: Stamp duty on a second home is higher, which angers buy-to-let investors.

items.definitionEn: the legal work of transferring ownership of a property
items.example: Slow conveyancing delayed the move by six weeks and cost another month's rent.

items.definitionEn: ownership of a building and the land it stands on, with no time limit
items.example: A freehold house avoids the ground rent that leaseholders must pay.

items.definitionPl: własność czasowa lokalu (najem wieczysty / prawo własności ograniczone czasem)
items.definitionEn: ownership of a flat or house for a fixed number of years, not of the land itself
items.example: A short leasehold can make a mortgage more expensive or impossible.

items.definitionEn: an annual fee a leaseholder pays to the landowner
items.example: Rising ground rent turned a cheap flat into a financial trap.

items.definitionEn: a lift in a building used for goods rather than residents
items.example: Furniture was taken up in the service lift so it would not scratch the hall.

items.definitionEn: the money a tenant pays regularly to live in a property they do not own
items.example: The rent went up by ten percent with no improvements to the flat.

items.definitionPl: refinansować hipotekę, wziąć nowy kredyt hipoteczny
items.definitionEn: to take out a new mortgage on a property you already own, often to get a better rate
items.example: They decided to remortgage when the fixed deal ended and rates fell.

items.definitionEn: the portion of a property's value that you own, after subtracting the mortgage
items.example: Years of repayments slowly built up equity they later used to move.

items.definitionEn: someone purchasing a home who has not owned one before
items.example: A first-time buyer often competes with investors who can pay in cash.

items.definitionEn: an arrangement in which two or more people rent a property together on equal terms
items.example: A joint tenancy means you may be liable if a flatmate stops paying.

items.definitionEn: a person who legally agrees to pay the rent if the tenant does not
items.example: Many students need a parent as guarantor before a landlord will sign.

items.definitionEn: a detailed list of a property's contents and condition at the start of a tenancy
items.example: Photograph every mark on the inventory or you may lose part of the deposit.

items.definitionEn: ordinary damage that happens through everyday use, not through negligence
items.example: A landlord cannot keep the deposit for reasonable wear and tear.

items.definitionEn: a non-profit organisation that provides rented homes at below-market rates
items.example: A housing association flat is more secure than a short private tenancy.

items.definitionEn: to rent out a room or flat that you yourself are renting from a landlord
items.example: You usually need written permission before you sublet a room to a classmate.

items.definitionEn: a person who rents a room in someone else's home, often sharing the kitchen
items.example: Taking in a lodger can help a homeowner cover a rising mortgage.

items.definitionEn: a term in a tenancy that allows either side to end the contract early after giving notice
items.example: Without a break clause you may pay rent until the end of the academic year.

items.definitionEn: an official rating of how energy-efficient a home is
items.example: Landlords must show an energy performance certificate before advertising a let.
